title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Labor share falling is just about technology and automation, not worker power

Rebuttal: Technology plays a role; machines and software shift income to capital. But other rich countries with the same technology haven't seen the same collapse, and research ties U.S. declines to falling union density and employer market power. BLS shows labor's share hit 52.8% in 2026, a record low since 1947. Policy and power matter.

Sources: BLS Productivity and Costs 2026, Economic Policy Institute

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Wages are rising faster than inflation, so workers are doing fine

Rebuttal: Nominal pay is up 4.6% and that beats 3.9% inflation. But real median weekly earnings rose only about $2 in a year, to $378 in 1982–84 dollars. And labor's share of income is at a record low. Workers are barely keeping pace while profits take the rest.

Sources: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings 2026, BLS Productivity and Costs 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Productivity gains always end up in workers' paychecks

Rebuttal: Over the long run some gains reach workers. But in 2025 productivity rose 2.2% while real hourly compensation rose 1.4%, and in spring 2026 real compensation fell at a 3.3% rate. Gains reach workers when workers have bargaining power to claim them.

Sources: BLS Productivity and Costs 2026, BLS Productivity and Costs March 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Wage theft is rare and mostly honest paperwork mistakes

Rebuttal: Some violations are mistakes, especially at small firms. But the Labor Department recovered more than $259 million for nearly 177,000 workers in fiscal 2025 alone, and EPI tallied over $1.5 billion recovered from 2021 to 2023. Patterns that large aren't typos.

Sources: DOL Wage and Hour Division 2026, Economic Policy Institute 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana doesn't need its own wage enforcement because federal law covers it

Rebuttal: Federal law does apply. But the federal Wage and Hour Division is small and stretched across the whole country. EPI found Louisiana is one of seven states that don't recover unpaid wages for workers. That leaves a gap bosses can exploit.

Sources: Economic Policy Institute 2025, DOL Wage and Hour Division 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Child labor laws are outdated and keep teens from learning to work

Rebuttal: Teens benefit from safe, legal jobs, and current law allows plenty. But the Labor Department found 5,272 minors working illegally in fiscal 2025, including 773 in hazardous jobs. The problem isn't too many rules. It's too many violations.

Sources: DOL child labor data FY2025, Economic Policy Institute 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Loosening child labor rules helps fill labor shortages

Rebuttal: Some employers do struggle to hire. But the answer is better pay and conditions for adults, not longer hours and riskier jobs for kids. States weakened protections while illegal child labor cases climbed to record levels.

Sources: Economic Policy Institute 2026, DOL child labor data FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Parents, not government, should decide whether kids work

Rebuttal: Parents should have a big say, and family farms have long exemptions. But child labor laws exist because employers, not parents, set hours and hazards. Arkansas dropped work permits in 2023, removing a basic check. Kids on overnight sanitation shifts didn't choose freely.

Sources: Arkansas Youth Hiring Act 2023, DOL child labor data FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: OSHA has enough inspectors; most employers follow the rules

Rebuttal: Many employers do. But the AFL-CIO calculates federal OSHA would need 191 years to inspect every workplace once, with one inspector per 93,877 workers. Rules without inspection are honor systems, and honor doesn't stop trench collapses.

Sources: AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026, OSHA staffing data

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: OSHA penalties are tough enough to deter bad employers

Rebuttal: Penalties can sting a small shop. But the median penalty in a worker death case was $16,550 in fiscal 2025, and only 144 death cases have been criminally prosecuted since 1970. For a large company, that's a rounding error.

Sources: AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026, OSHA enforcement data

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: A federal heat standard would be a one-size-fits-all burden

Rebuttal: Workplaces differ, and a good rule must be flexible. OSHA's 2024 proposal used heat index triggers and let employers write their own plans. The AFL-CIO estimates about 530 workers died from heat in 2024. Water, rest and shade aren't a burden.

Sources: OSHA proposed rule, Aug. 2024, AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Workers in the South are used to the heat

Rebuttal: People acclimate somewhat, and Gulf workers know heat. But acclimation has limits, and heat illness kills experienced workers too. Seven states have heat standards; Louisiana has none. Being tough isn't protection.

Sources: Ogletree Deakins 2026, AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Most workers already get paid sick leave

Rebuttal: Most do: 81% of private workers had it in March 2026. But for the lowest-paid quarter of workers it's 63%, and in leisure and hospitality just 58%. The workers most likely to spread illness are the least able to stay home.

Sources: BLS National Compensation Survey 2026, BLS Employee Benefits 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Paid sick leave mandates hurt small businesses

Rebuttal: Small businesses have thin margins and that's real. Many state laws exempt the smallest firms or phase in slowly. Meanwhile 95% of the best-paid workers already have it. Low-wage workers deserve the same basic protection.

Sources: BLS National Compensation Survey 2026, State paid sick leave laws

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Low-wage workers just don't save for retirement

Rebuttal: Some people struggle to save at any income. But only 48% of the lowest-paid quarter of private workers even had access to a retirement plan in 2026, versus 92% at the top. You can't join a plan you're not offered.

Sources: BLS National Compensation Survey 2026, BLS Employee Benefits 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Noncompetes protect trade secrets and investment in training

Rebuttal: Employers have real interests in protecting secrets. But trade secret law and nondisclosure agreements already do that. Noncompetes mainly block workers from taking better jobs. The FTC dropped its ban in 2025, leaving workers to state law.

Sources: FTC Sept. 2025, Louisiana R.S. 23:921

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: App drivers prefer contractor status, so the government should leave it alone

Rebuttal: Many gig workers value flexibility, and polls show it. But flexibility and labor protections aren't opposites. Contractors lose minimum wage, overtime and unemployment insurance. The Labor Department stopped enforcing its stronger misclassification rule in 2025.

Sources: DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1, DOL proposed rule Feb. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Every minimum wage increase costs low-wage workers their jobs

Rebuttal: Very large, fast hikes can reduce hours in some places, and economists debate the size. But 19 states raised wages on Jan. 1, 2026, giving 8.3 million workers about $5 billion a year. States with higher minimums have kept growing jobs.

Sources: Economic Policy Institute Dec. 2025, BLS state employment data

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's cost of living is low, so $7.25 is fine here

Rebuttal: Costs are lower than in Seattle. But $7.25 full-time is $15,080 a year, and the federal minimum hasn't changed since 2009 while prices have. Louisiana has one of the highest poverty rates in the country. Low cost isn't no cost.

Sources: DOL minimum wage history, Economic Policy Institute Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Few people actually earn the minimum wage

Rebuttal: True, a small share earn exactly $7.25. But the minimum sets the floor for millions earning just above it. EPI counts 60.2 million workers in states still at $7.25. When the floor stays stuck, the whole bottom stays stuck.

Sources: Economic Policy Institute Dec. 2025, BLS Characteristics of Minimum Wage Workers

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Strikes hurt the economy and the public

Rebuttal: Strikes do disrupt service, and workers lose pay too. But strikes are rare, about 30 major ones in 2025, and they often win safer staffing and better pay. Health care workers struck over staffing that endangers patients.

Sources: BLS Major Work Stoppages 2026, Cornell ILR Labor Action Tracker 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Unions are a thing of the past; workers don't want them

Rebuttal: Union membership is far below its peak. But 306,800 workers joined major strikes in 2025, up 13%, and unions still won about 70% of NLRB elections. Interest is real. The obstacles are employer opposition and weak law.

Sources: BLS Major Work Stoppages 2026, Center for American Progress 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Southern workers don't strike because they're satisfied

Rebuttal: Many Southern workers do like their jobs. But Cornell counted only 43 Southern work stoppages in 2025, the fewest of any region, alongside the lowest pay floors. Right-to-work laws and fear of retaliation explain quiet better than satisfaction.

Sources: Cornell ILR Labor Action Tracker 2025, Economic Policy Institute Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Firing Gwynne Wilcox was a lawful use of presidential power

Rebuttal: Courts have largely sided with the president. The D.C. Circuit upheld the removal, and in June 2026 the Supreme Court overruled Humphrey's Executor. But legal isn't the same as good. The board went 345 days without a quorum, stalling cases for fired workers.

Sources: Trump v. Slaughter 2026, Center for American Progress 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The NLRB quorum gap didn't affect ordinary workers

Rebuttal: Regional offices kept running elections. But without a quorum the board couldn't decide appeals, and elections fell 30% in 2025. A worker fired for organizing waited longer for a ruling. Delay favors employers.

Sources: Center for American Progress 2026, Proskauer Rose 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Union elections falling shows workers are losing interest

Rebuttal: Elections dropped from 2,124 to 1,498 in 2025. But the shutdown closed regional offices and the board lacked a quorum. Unions still won 69.8% of votes held. The pipeline was clogged; demand didn't vanish.

Sources: Center for American Progress 2026, NLRB data

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Right-to-work protects workers' freedom

Rebuttal: No worker should be forced to join a union, and federal law already says so. Right-to-work lets workers get union representation without paying for it, draining resources. Louisiana, right-to-work since 1976, had a 4.4% union rate in 2025, less than half the nation's.

Sources: BLS Union Members by State 2026, Louisiana R.S. 23:981

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana wages are low because of low productivity

Rebuttal: Some sectors are low-productivity. But Baton Rouge production workers averaged $33.04 an hour in 2025, above the national $24.81. Where workers have leverage, pay follows. New Orleans waiters averaged $11.55. The difference is power.

Sources: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages Aug. 2026, BLS OEWS Baton Rouge 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tourism jobs are entry-level and aren't meant to support families

Rebuttal: Some are first jobs. But many hospitality workers are adults supporting families for decades. New Orleans pays 12.5% below the national average wage. A city that earns billions from visitors can pay the people who serve them.

Sources: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages Aug. 2026, BLS National Compensation Survey 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Immigrants drive down wages for American workers

Rebuttal: Employers sometimes use vulnerable workers to cut costs. That's the real issue. Foreign-born workers earned 85.7% of native-born pay in 2025. When bosses can underpay anyone, they underpay everyone. Equal rights and enforcement protect all of us.

Sources: BLS Foreign-born Workers 2026, BLS Usual Weekly Earnings 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The H-2A program protects guest workers with required wages and housing

Rebuttal: H-2A does require set wages, housing and transportation, which is more than some farmworkers get. But workers are tied to one employer and can lose their status if fired. 398,258 positions were certified in fiscal 2025. Protections on paper need enforcement and the freedom to speak.

Sources: DOL OFLC FY2025, DOL H-2A rules

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Prison work teaches incarcerated people skills and responsibility

Rebuttal: Good job training in prison helps people succeed after release. But field labor for 2 to 4 cents an hour after three years unpaid isn't job training. It's cheap labor. Pay a fair wage and teach real trades.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator May 2026, Louisiana DPS&C policy

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Angola's farm line is safe; a federal judge said so

Rebuttal: The judge did find in May 2026 that the state's heat measures met the legal standard under a 5th Circuit precedent. But he said he could not force a fix, and advocates called it a victory without a remedy. Meeting a low bar isn't the same as being humane.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator May 2026, Parker v. Hooper, 5th Cir.

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Work deaths are falling, so safety is improving

Rebuttal: The national fatality rate dipped to 3.3 per 100,000 in 2024, and that's progress. But Louisiana's rate was 5.1, Latino deaths here nearly doubled, and the young worker death rate doubled since 2022. Averages hide the people still dying.

Sources: BLS CFOI Louisiana 2026, AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Older workers choose to keep working because they enjoy it

Rebuttal: Some do, and good for them. But workers 65 and older die on the job at 9.1 per 100,000, nearly three times the overall rate, and many lack retirement plans. For many, it's need, not choice.

Sources: AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026, BLS National Compensation Survey 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The gender pay gap is explained by job choices

Rebuttal: Occupation and hours explain part of it. But women's median weekly pay was 82.0% of men's in spring 2026, and gaps persist within the same jobs. Transparent union pay scales shrink the gap most.

Sources: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings 2026, BLS Union Members 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Racial pay gaps reflect education differences, not discrimination

Rebuttal: Education explains some of the gap. But Black workers earned $1,029 a week versus $1,268 for white workers in spring 2026, and research finds gaps at every education level. Contracts with set wages narrow them.

Sources: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings 2026, Economic Policy Institute

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Injuries are mostly caused by careless workers

Rebuttal: Workers make mistakes; everyone does. But safety science puts the responsibility on employers to design out hazards. The AFL-CIO estimates job injuries and illnesses cost $177 to $354 billion a year. Blaming workers doesn't fix a missing guardrail.

Sources: AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026, OSHA hierarchy of controls

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Employers should be trusted to report injuries honestly

Rebuttal: Many do. But the AFL-CIO estimates the real toll is 5 to 7.5 million injuries a year in private industry, versus about 3.1 million reported. Underreporting keeps rates looking good and workers uncompensated.

Sources: AFL-CIO Death on the Job 2026, BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: State-level minimum wages create a confusing patchwork

Rebuttal: Different rates do complicate things for multistate employers. But the patchwork exists because Congress has left the federal floor at $7.25 since 2009. Washington pays $17.13, Louisiana $7.25. Raise the federal floor and the patchwork shrinks.

Sources: Economic Policy Institute Dec. 2025, DOL minimum wage history

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Family leave should be up to employers, not government

Rebuttal: Some employers offer generous leave voluntarily. But only 49% of private workers had paid family leave in March 2026. Leaving it to employers leaves half the workforce choosing between family and paycheck.

Sources: BLS National Compensation Survey 2026, State paid family leave programs

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Reclassifying gig workers would end flexible schedules

Rebuttal: Some companies say so. But employees can have flexible schedules, and many do. The real change is minimum wage, overtime and unemployment insurance. Misclassification shifts costs from companies to workers.

Sources: DOL proposed rule Feb. 2026, DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Labor share data overstates the problem because benefits aren't counted

Rebuttal: Fair concern, but BLS labor share counts total compensation, including benefits. Even counting health insurance and retirement, workers' share hit a record low of 52.8% in 2026.

Sources: BLS Productivity and Costs 2026, BLS technical notes

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Workers can just switch jobs if their pay is low

Rebuttal: Job switching does raise pay for some. But noncompetes, lack of savings and tied visas limit mobility. The FTC abandoned its noncompete ban in 2025, and guest workers can't freely change employers. Exit isn't always an option. Organizing is.

Sources: FTC Sept. 2025, DOL OFLC FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Back wages recovered prove enforcement works fine

Rebuttal: Recoveries are good news, and fiscal 2025's $259 million was the most since 2019. But that's about $1,465 per worker, and EPI says recoveries are a small part of total theft. Recovery after the fact isn't prevention.

Sources: DOL Wage and Hour Division 2026, Economic Policy Institute 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Child labor penalties are already harsh

Rebuttal: Penalties did rise to about $37.2 million in fiscal 2025. But that's spread across 976 cases, and for big meatpackers or contractors it's a cost of doing business. Strong penalties plus enforcement deter; light ones invite repeat offenses.

Sources: DOL child labor data FY2025, Economic Policy Institute 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Labor law should be neutral, not pro-union

Rebuttal: Neutrality sounds fair. But the National Labor Relations Act says its purpose is to encourage collective bargaining. With a record-low labor share and a weakened NLRB, neutrality in practice means employers win by default.

Sources: National Labor Relations Act Sec. 1, BLS Productivity and Costs 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Strikes rarely win anything

Rebuttal: Some strikes fail, and workers pay a price. But many win: health care workers have won staffing gains and machinists won raises. 306,800 workers struck in 2025 because it works often enough to be worth the risk.

Sources: BLS Major Work Stoppages 2026, Economic Policy Institute 2026
